title: Taiwan's war drills showcased a new strike drone class that Ukraine used to smash Russia this year
description: Taiwan's navy deployed two fixed-wing propeller drones, which officials described as "mid-size suicide drones" that were locally built.
fullText:
Taiwan showcased two midsize strike drones above its southwest coast on Saturday.

Their designs and descriptions draw easy comparisons to Ukraine's mid-range drones.

Such drones likely give Taiwan the ability to cheaply hit a Chinese invasion force over the horizon.

TSOYING, TAIWAN — Taiwan's navy deployed two medium-class strike drones on Saturday for the island's biggest annual military exercise, and their designs resemble those of the loitering munitions giving Ukraine fresh wins against Russia this year.

The pair of fixed-wing, propeller-driven drones appeared during a littoral combat drill simulating an attack on Tsoying, Taiwan's southwest coast.

It was the first time these drones were shown at the Han Kuang exercise, Taiwan's annual rehearsals against a Chinese invasion.

As the drones loitered for about 30 minutes above the beach, Taiwanese military officials described them to reporters as "medium-size suicide drones," adding they were locally built. The island's National Chung-Shan Institute of Science and Technology designs and manufactures the vast majority of Taiwan's homegrown weapons.

"The drone used was provided by the Armament Bureau to the navy for testing purpose," a spokesperson for Taiwan's navy told Business Insider.

They declined to comment on the drone's specifications or whether its design was influenced in any way by the recent wars in Ukraine or the Middle East.

The one-way drones were not shown attempting to launch an attack, and it's unclear whether they represent Taiwan's final designs for the aircraft.

Ukraine has been using similar fixed-wing drones to attack Russian forces roughly 30 to 300 km behind the front lines this year, mainly disrupting supply routes that the Kremlin has relied on to funnel resources to the war.

Tsoying, where Taiwan hosts its largest naval base, is about 295 km, or 183 miles, from mainland China.

"The desire to employ more medium-range drones fits into things that Taiwan has learned from Ukraine," said Bryce Barros, a visiting fellow at the Institute for National Defense and Security Research, a Taipei think-tank backed by the Taiwanese government.

Mid-range drones would fill a gap in Taiwan's littoral defense with a cheaper way to strike Chinese forces or weapons from "over-the-horizon" as they approach the island, Barros said.

Unlike Ukraine's plains and forests, Taiwan's littoral defense covers a strait notorious for bad winds and volatile sea states, suggesting that Taipei may want its own drone built to withstand poor weather.

Instead of air defense systems or supply trucks like in Ukraine or Crimea, Taiwan's mid-range drones would likely target slow-moving vessels transporting troops or weapons, Barros added.

"A range of 40 kilometers to 60 kilometers would be very useful for a whole host of different platforms, anything to make it more difficult for the PLA to start getting into Taiwan's territorial waters," he said, referring to the People's Liberation Army.

Taiwan's government has said that it plans to produce 100,000 drones a month by 2030. In June, its national defense ministry proposed a $6.6 billion budget to procure over 210,000 domestically produced attack, reconnaissance, and sea drones.

It's all part of the island's emerging "hellscape" strategy, which aims to hamper Chinese forces attempting to cross the Taiwan Strait by flooding it with thousands of aerial, surface, and underwater drones.

The littoral drills on Saturday, attended by Taiwanese president Lai Ching-te, also featured naval special forces deploying in the island's homegrown M109 Skyship rigid-hull inflatable boats.

Taiwan's navy and coast guard launched rapid sorties with four of its older, 170-ton Kuang Hua-6 missile boats and at least one Anping-class patrol vessel — a newer, 750-ton catamaran that can be fitted with anti-ship missiles during wartime.

The Han Kuang exercise, which lasts 10 days and 9 nights this year, features island-wide drills to simulate how Taiwanese forces and civilian institutions would respond to Chinese gray-zone tactics and an invasion.

August 10, 2026: This story was updated to reflect the romanized spelling of Tsoying.

If you enjoyed this story, be sure to follow Business Insider on Yahoo.

title: Moscow, Kyiv assassins hunt weapons bosses as Ukraine war spills beyond the battlefield
description: Draganfly CEO Cameron Chell says drone company leaders are now primary targets as Russia and Ukraine race for battlefield AI and autonomy advantages.
fullText:
A dangerous new front is emerging in the Russia-Ukraine war as attackers and alleged intelligence operatives increasingly target executives and engineers developing the cutting-edge drone technology that is reshaping the battlefield, industry experts warned Sunday.

The attacks include an Aug. 4 car bombing near Yekaterinburg that critically injured Vladimir Tkachuk, head of Russian drone manufacturer Uraldronzavod, and killed his driver, according to Russian state news agency TASS, The Associated Press reported.

His company produces the "Upyr," or "Ghoul," a first-person-view attack drone used by Russian forces in Ukraine.

'A New Kind Of War': Inside Ukraine's Hidden Factories Mass-producing Combat Drones

Days earlier, Andrei Cherezov, head of another Russian drone company, was shot three times in Tula overnight July 28-29 in an apparent assassination attempt, according to Ukrainian outlet Pravda. Authorities have not publicly attributed either attack to Ukraine.

Draganfly CEO Cameron Chell told Fox News Digital that the rise in attacks comes as Russia and Ukraine race for an edge in drone warfare, making the relatively small number of people responsible for developing new technology increasingly important targets.

"When you can't take out all the distributed infrastructure, drone manufacturing leadership becomes the primary target," Chell said.

"These strikes in Russia and Ukraine and Germany on founders, leaders, engineers of defense and, in particular, drone-type companies are down to drones and these companies having such an impact themselves."

Ukraine's Battlefield Is Transforming The Future Of Nato

"Because drone technology evolves rapidly — often with significant iterations occurring every 10 to 30 days — targeting a key engineer, founder, or product lead creates immediate operational disruptions on the battlefield."

"Taking out a particular engineer or taking out a particular leader can set a very important weapons program back quite some time and disrupt shipments to the front line," Chell added.

German authorities have also arrested two suspected operatives accused of spying on a Bavarian drone manufacturer for Russian intelligence, while reports this month said the alleged operation included preparations to target company executive Stefan Thumann, according to Germany's Die Zeit.

The case follows a reported 2024 plot disrupted by U.S. and German intelligence to target Rheinmetall CEO Armin Papperger.

Zelenskyy Announces 'The Future Is Here' After War's First All-robot Capture

Chell said as Ukraine and Russia push toward artificial intelligence and autonomous weapons systems, engineers developing those technologies are more strategically important.

"What we see in the Ukraine-Russia conflict is nobody in the loop — total autonomy is the direction things are going because it moves with more speed and precision," Chell said.

"AI and total autonomy are the big innovations for the next 18 months, so a potential reason we could see more targeted activity against leaders is because Ukrainians have that technology advantage."

"Targeting small drone companies is a relatively easy operation compared to targeting individuals in state-run weapons programs," he said.

"It is a fairly inexpensive, low-risk tactic for intelligence agencies that yields an immediate impact on the battlefield, and that's why we've seen this tactic."

"It is a very interesting turn or tactic that's being played by both sides here."

Chell highlighted how Russia and Ukraine approach such plots differently.

"I wouldn't suggest one side has an advantage over the other in terms of tactics, but psychologically, it has a deeper effect on the Russian side," Chell said.

Ukraine Unleashes More Than 400 Drones Near Moscow In One Of War's Biggest Attacks

"The volume of drone advantage will remain with the Russians for the foreseeable future, but the innovation of drones, tactics, and technology lies with the Ukrainians right now."

"Ukraine faces an existential threat, so they are ready for anything. Their tactics tend to be much more blunt — a direct shooter in a hallway or a car bomb," he added.

"The Russian tactics tend to be much more state-organized, using old Cold War tactics: low-level contacts, extensive intelligence and surveillance ahead of time, and inserting into other countries like Germany," he said.

"The Russians have a long-standing, well-established intelligence infrastructure dating back to World War II and the Cold War."

Trump Is Proving That The Way To Better Our Military Is To Secure Our Supply Chains

As the drone manufacturing industry takes greater precautions, Chell maintained that threats against companies and individuals in the defense supply chain are receiving increased scrutiny.

"We are very cognizant of it, and we're in contact with the proper authorities to make sure we're taking precautions on both a cyber and physical level to ensure we're at less risk," he said.

"We certainly don't take anything for granted."

"There are training and programs in place to ensure executives have a level of safety, primarily around awareness, cybersecurity, and physical location protection," Chell added before stating that the attacks and attempted assassinations have "heightened the conversation around it."

"We as an industry are taking it with a measured amount more seriously," he said.

title: Syria will take back control from Russia of 2 key Mediterranean bases under a new deal
description: Russian forces in Syria will give up control of two strategic bases on the Mediterranean coast, which will be used as joint Russia-Syrian training centers under a new agreement between the two countri...
fullText:
DAMASCUS, Syria (AP) — Russian forces in Syria will give up control of two strategic bases on the Mediterranean coast, which will be used as joint Russia-Syrian training centers under a new agreement between the two countries, Syria's Foreign Ministry said Sunday.

Russia was the top political and military ally of ousted President Bashar Assad during the country's civil war between 2011 and 2024. Assad was ousted in December 2024 by Islamist insurgents led by current interim President Ahmad al-Sharaa and has since fled into exile in Russia.

Throughout the conflict, the Hmeimem air base and the Tartus naval base were key Russian military outposts in the eastern Mediterranean.

Under the new agreement between Damascus and Moscow, Syria will take control of the Hmeimem air base and the commercial berth at Tartus port as part of its civil administration. The military facilities at both sites will become "joint training" centers, the Foreign Ministry said.

The new arrangements represent a "reorganizing of the Russian presence" along Syria's coast, the ministry said.

"This move marks the most significant development since negotiations began approximately a year and a half ago, paving the way for a new phase in Syrian-Russian relations," the statement read.

Russia did not immediately comment on the agreement.

Moscow did not interfere during the lightning insurgency that led to Assad's overthrow, but it provided the longtime Syrian leader and his family asylum. After Assad's ouster Russian troops remaining in Syria gradually left the country except for those stationed at the bases.

Syria's new leadership has aimed to maintain strong bilateral ties with Moscow. Al-Sharaa has visited President Vladimir Putin in Moscow twice since taking power, with the two Mediterranean bases being key points of discussion.

Since Assad's ouster, Syria has also bolstered its ties with the United States, Europe, and neighboring Arab countries that had cut ties with Damascus during Assad's crackdown on protests. Washington has lifted most of its crippling sanctions on the country, and French President Emmanuel Macron made a visit to Syria in July during which he announced that the two countries would appoint respective ambassadors for the first time in 14 years.

Aug 9 (Reuters) - Syria and Russia reached a memorandum of understanding to settle the future of Russian bases ‌at Tartous and Hmeimim following 18 months of intensive ‌negotiations, the Syrian foreign ministry said on Sunday, according to the Syrian state ​news agency.

The ministry said the Syrian state would take over management of civilian facilities, including Hmeimim airport and the commercial berth at Tartous port, allowing them to be gradually integrated into the country's ‌civilian administration.

It said military ⁠facilities would be repurposed as joint training and qualification centres under new arrangements preserving the interests ⁠of both sides, with the transition to be completed within three months.

Russia's naval facility at Tartous and Hmeimim air base have long ​been Moscow's ​principal military footholds in the ​Mediterranean and Middle East.

Their future ‌has been the subject of negotiations with Syria's new leadership since former President Bashar al-Assad was ousted in December 2024.

In a separate statement, Syria's General Authority for Ports and Customs said Syria would take over the commercial sites previously operated by Russia ‌at Tartous port, including Pier No. ​4 and its associated warehouses and ​facilities.

The two sides said at the time the hub would remain under Syrian ​control, with all ‌operations subject to approval by Syria's General Authority for Ports ​and Customs.

title: A Russian retail giant’s warehouse burns after Ukraine's latest long-range drone attack
description: Ukrainian long-range drones hit a warehouse of Russia’s biggest online retailer in the Ural Mountains, more than 2,000 kilometers (1,200 miles) from the two countries’ border, local officials and the ...
fullText:
Ukrainian long-range drones hit a warehouse of Russia's biggest online retailer in the Ural Mountains, more than 2,000 kilometers (1,200 miles) from the two countries' border, local officials and the company said Friday.

Ukraine has regularly hit targets in the distant Urals this year and has even struck a Russian oil refinery in western Siberia, nearly 2,500 kilometers (1,550 miles) from the border. The attacks are examples of how Kyiv has used drone innovation as a key part of its response to the invasion by its much bigger enemy more than four years ago.

Its successes have drawn international interest and drone cooperation agreements with nine countries, with further deals being negotiated with 15 other countries, according to Kyiv officials.

Wildberries said its warehouse in Yekaterinburg, Russia's fourth-largest city, was set ablaze by the attack. Most merchandise wasn't damaged, the company said, unlike at some of the more than a dozen other Wildberries depots struck by Ukraine in recent weeks that have burned down.

The regional governor, Denis Pasler, said three drones hit the warehouse's roof. Artyom Zhoga, the Kremlin's representative in the region, said that 800 people were evacuated from the warehouse and nobody was hurt.

Kyiv is trying to rattle the Russian public and the Kremlin with the attacks.

Russian President Vladimir Putin chaired a meeting Friday of the country's Security Council. He said in televised opening remarks that the meeting would focus on additional measures to "strengthen … protection of infrastructure facilities" but gave no further details.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is pushing for his country to keep up the pace of technological development, especially in air defense systems to help stop Russian ballistic missiles that are exploiting Ukraine's shortage of American-made Patriot interceptor missiles and battering civilian areas.

A joint European anti-ballistic development program is already underway, Zelenskyy said late Thursday, with 10 countries engaged in developing an anti-ballistic shield. Europe is concerned about Moscow's ambitions on the continent beyond Ukraine.

"Ukraine is capable of producing its (anti-ballistic) missile and launcher, while our partners will provide the necessary components and critical elements — radars, sensors, and everything else required," Zelenskyy said on social media. "An anti-ballistic program of our own — one that is truly large-scale — will greatly benefit everyone in Europe."

At the same time, Ukraine is working on manufacturing its own ballistic missiles to use against Russia. "The tests have shown strong potential. We need to turn this into a real weapon," Zelenskyy said.

Ukrainian front-line defenses in eastern regions, meanwhile, remain under strain as Russia's bigger army looks for a breakthrough after months of minimal advances that Western analysts and officials say have had a high cost for Moscow in troop casualties.

Ukraine has been evacuating children from Kramatorsk, one of the four eastern Donetsk region cities that make up the Ukrainian so-called Fortress Belt. The line of four large and heavily defended cities, about 50 kilometers (30 miles) long, has been key to denying Moscow its goal of seizing Ukraine's industrial heartland.

The head of the Donetsk region's regional military administration, Vadym Filashkin, said Friday that more than 800 people, including 91 children, were evacuated over the previous 24 hours.

Ukraine has been deploying midrange strike drones to disrupt Russia's supply lines and slow its advance.

Zelenskyy said that the recently appointed commander-in-chief of the Ukrainian armed forces, Maj. Gen. Mykhailo Drapatyi, reported to him Friday about the military situation in Donetsk.

He said in a social media post that they reached "an understanding of how to strengthen" Ukraine's defenses there but gave no details.

Russia's air defenses downed 203 Ukrainian drones from late Thursday through early Friday, the Defense Ministry in Moscow said.

Over the past week, the Russian military struck 31 bulk cargo vessels and three tugboats that operated "in the interests of the Ukrainian armed forces," it said.

It added that late Thursday two ships were hit by Geran-4 drones in the Black Sea east and southeast of Odesa and one was struck in the Ukrainian port of Chornomorsk.

In other attacks, the ministry said that the military hit a facility assembling long-range drones in Okhtyrka in the Sumy region on Thursday. It also released a video of a train purportedly carrying military equipment struck by a Geran drone and then an Iskander ballistic missile near Vyshneve in the Dnipropetrovsk region.

Meanwhile, Russia attacked Ukraine with 147 long-range strike drones overnight, according to the Ukrainian air force.

In Ukraine's northern Sumy region, a Russian drone struck a busy market Friday morning, wounding 10 people, authorities said.

Russia also launched glide bombs and drones of various types at the regional capital, according to the head of regional administration, Oleh Hryhorov.

The attack targeted residential buildings, transport and infrastructure, wounding two people, he said.

Follow the AP's coverage of the war in Ukraine at https://apnews.com/hub/russia-ukraine

title: Crowded Russian beach descends into chaos after alleged Ukrainian drone incident kills 7, including 4 children
description: A projectile struck a crowded Russian Black Sea beach Monday, killing seven people, including four children, and injuring 58. Russia blamed a Ukrainian drone attack as video captured the deadly impact...
fullText:
Vacationers were sent scrambling for safety Monday after a projectile struck a crowded beach in a Russian Black Sea resort town, killing seven people, including four children, and injuring dozens more, officials said.

Video footage captured the incident in the village of Arkhipo-Osipovka near Gelendzhik, where the beach was packed with visitors at the time of the strike.

The Russian Mission in Geneva said in a post on X that the "bloody attack" was carried out by a drone launched by Ukraine, accusing Kyiv of targeting civilians.

Ukraine Launches What Appears To Be One Of Its Largest Drone Attacks Against Russia: Report

"The attack targeted civilian infrastructure. Emergency and special services are working at the crash site," regional Gov. Veniamin Kondratyev said in a post on Telegram.

"What happened today is a targeted attack by the Kyiv regime against civilians who have no connection to the military infrastructure. This cynical and inhumane terrorist attack against children cannot be justified."

Ukraine Unleashes More Than 400 Drones Near Moscow In One Of War's Biggest Attacks

Andriy Kovalenko, an officer with Ukraine's Defense Forces, disputed Russia's account, saying the deaths were directly caused by Russian air defenses that intercepted a drone, sending debris onto the beach.

"Russian air defense shot down a drone over people lying on the beach," Kovalenko said on Telegram.

In the video, sounds resembling gunfire were heard just seconds before a drone struck the beach, causing a fireball explosion that sent bystanders screaming. As the gunfire was heard, the drone appeared to veer sharply before diving toward the beach.

Preliminary Russian reports also found that several of the deaths were caused by "falling drone debris," Kondratyev said.

Zelenskyy Says Putin 'Lost The Initiative' As Ukraine's Tech Industry Reshapes The War

In another Telegram post, Kovalenko indicated that Ukraine uses its weapons against Russian military-industrial infrastructure to affect Moscow's ability to finance the war.

He further accused Russian President Vladimir Putin of creating an "illusion" that Russia would remain safe from the war by downplaying daily explosions as falling debris, limiting air raid warnings, and positioning air defenses near populated areas such as the Black Sea resort.

"Putin deliberately killed these people. Because if he had not started the war and struck Ukraine, they would be alive," Kovalenko said.

"It was Putin, his air defense, who killed these Russians. His decisions in response to their decisions launched a chain of death for Russians."

title: Ukrainian attacks on Wildberries strike at heart of Russia Inc
Opinion - This winter, Putin will feed even more of Russia’s youth into the meat grinder
description: Russian President Vladimir Putin is a cornered man. Ukraine, especially through its deep-strike drones and ballistic missiles, is bringing Putin’s special military operation home to the city confines ...
fullText:
Russian President Vladimir Putin is a cornered man. Ukraine, especially through its deep-strike drones and ballistic missiles, is bringing Putin's special military operation home to the city confines of Moscow and Saint Petersburg.

As of this writing, 15 distribution hubs of Wildberries — Russia's equivalent of Amazon, which is frequently used to supply troops with equipment the Russian state fails to supply — have been hit or destroyed by Ukraine. Likewise, most of Putin's largest oil refineries, including one as far away as Siberia, have been struck.

Billowy black smoke from burning Wildberries and uncertainty at the gas pump are putting domestic pressure on the Kremlin in ways never felt since the war began in February 2022.

Putin must either go big or go home. Going home probably means the end of his regime, so going big in Ukraine is really his only option. All signs indicate that he intends to do so this winter, whatever the cost.

Putin is not going to use nuclear weapons, although he can be counted on to threaten and bluff with them. No — going big for him means doubling, if not tripling down on his meat grinder approach to the war in Ukraine. Mass infantry attacks are his military strategy. If a Russian operation fails on the frontlines, his typical response is simply to try it again with larger numbers. This is why, in the first half of 2026, Russia has suffered roughly eight casualties the for every one it has inflicted on Ukraine.

The paradox of Putin's stratagem is that, during the first four years of the war, as he has ramped up his investment of Russian lives in the conflict, he has gotten diminishing returns. Russian casualties, dead and wounded, are fast-approaching 1.5 million, with little accomplished on the battlefield.

The Institute for the Study of War estimates that as of late July, Russia had gained only 81 square kilometers of Ukrainian territory this calendar year. In fact, since January 2023, the Kremlin has seized only about 5 to 6 square kilometers while incurring 925 casualties each day on average since 2023.

Undeterred, Putin will keep squeezing harder/ With the repeated failures of his spring and summer ground offensives, he will weaponize the coming winter once again, calculating that he will enjoy a new strategic opening in the compounding Patriot interceptor shortage in Ukraine and Europe's indecision over establishing a No-Fly Zone.

In July, Moscow increased its widescale aerial attacks on Ukraine. According to Militarnyi, Russia fired "107 ballistic missiles and 20 3M22 Zircon [hypersonic] missiles," which was a significant surge from June. Likewise, according to Ukrainian Colonel Oleksandr Zaruba, Russian drone attacks have substantially increased as well "to wage a war of attrition against Ukraine's air defenses."

Although Russia is firing off missiles faster than it can produce them, it has apparently struck a new deal with North Korea to augment its ballistic missile stockpile. "A North Korean missile unit has begun deploying to western Russia and could be equipped with 120 ballistic missiles and six launchers for strikes against Ukraine," Reuters reports.

So Putin is again betting on destroying Ukraine's critical infrastructure, including its electrical power grid, to bring the country to its knees during the coldest months of the coming year. This follows the same old playbook: Hit the grid, pressure the population, then launch another spring offensive to seize all of the Donbas. This is supposed to force Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and his generals to capitulate.

But here's the problem: Another large-scale Russian military operation will require a new mobilization of conscripts and reserves. Russian casualties in Ukraine so far in 2026 continue to exceed recruitment of new soldiers.

Putin is unlikely to issue new mobilization orders until after the Russian Duma elections in September. That means the new Russian conscripts or reserve call-ups used in 2027 will be hastily trained and poorly equipped. They will be no match for Ukraine's established kill zones or the country's battle-hardened armed forces on the frontlines.

Putin is desperate for a win in the Donbas. Will he get it? Almost certainly not. But he will bleed hundreds of thousands of Russian soldiers in the process of finding out.

Mark Toth writes on national security and foreign policy. Col. (Ret.) Jonathan Sweet served 30 years as a military intelligence officer and led the U.S. European Command Intelligence Engagement Division from 2012 to 2014. They are the cofounders of INTREP360 and the INTREP360 Intelligence Report on Substack.

title: Terrifying 'human safaris' on display in shocking video that reveals depths of Russia's deadly campaign
description: Video shows a Russian drone stalking a vegetable vendor through a Kherson market before detonating near him, in what Zelenskyy calls a "safari."
fullText:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy accused Russia of going "mad" following the release of a video showing a Ukrainian vegetable vendor being stalked by a Russian military drone before the drone exploded near him.

The incident occurred on Aug. 4 at a Kherson market located in Southern Ukraine. Footage released by the Kherson Regional Military Administration shows a drone hovering near a man standing beside a minibus before following him as he moves behind the bus. Moments later the drone dives toward the minibus and explodes near its front, detonating close to where the man is standing.

"A Russian drone deliberately hunted down a man selling vegetables and detonated right next to him," Zelenskyy wrote on X in a post including the video. "The Russians even admitted to the crime, showing zero regret and openly boasting about tormenting people. The man was wounded in the blast. Every single day, ordinary people in Kherson face these Russian "safaris."

Moscow Bombing Exposes Potential Security Gaps Around Putin's Military Elite, Expert Says

The street vendor, identified as 52-year-old Yuriy, survived the near-fatal encounter, which Ukrainian authorities describe as part of a pattern of Russian drone attacks that track and target civilians — a practice they have dubbed "human safaris."

Speaking from a hospital bed, Yuriy told BBC that he and his wife were setting up their stall when he heard the drone buzzing nearby. His wife had run away, and the drone zeroed in on Yuriy, who pulled out vegetables to show that he did not have a weapon.

"It could see that I had tomatoes out, some cucumbers and eggplants laid out on the floor," Yuriy told BBC. "It even ducked under the umbrella when I was running away round the other side."

Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha called the attack a "barbaric war crime," demanding international intervention.

Why Trump Is Downplaying Reports Russia And China Are Helping Iran

Zelenskyy argued that everyone should see the video to make clear what Russia is capable of, arguing that President Vladimir Putin won't stop with Ukraine.

"This is not just about Ukraine," Zelenskyy wrote. "Russia's campaign against human life must be stopped here in Ukraine before it spreads further. Finland and Kazakhstan, the Baltic states and Poland, the countries of the South Caucasus, Romania, and Moldova — all should work together to ensure real security guarantees and bring Russia's war to an end."

"Peace is needed, which requires cooperation among everyone in the world who truly values peace," Zelenskyy wrote.

Ukraine's Prosecutor General's Office says authorities have opened 5,303 criminal cases into drone attacks on civilian targets in the Kherson region. The office says the attacks have killed 287 civilians and wounded 2,549 others, including 41 children.

Ukraine Seeks More U.s. Patriot Interceptors As Bomb Shelter Probe Deepens

Prosecutors said the attacks appeared to be part of a systematic campaign, with FPV drones repeatedly striking civilians in public places, homes, transport hubs and civilian vehicles, and in some cases launching follow-up attacks after emergency crews arrived.

The release of the chilling video comes a year after a one-year-old boy was killed by a Russian drone in the Kherson region while playing in his playpen in his grandmother's backyard.

title: Ukraine accuses Russia of war crime after video shows drone attacking vegetable seller in Kherson
description: KYIV, Aug 4 () - Ukraine on Tuesday accused Russia of committing a war crime after a video was released showing a drone chasing down and wounding a vegetable seller in the southern Ukrainian city of K...
fullText:
KYIV, Aug 4 (Reuters) - Ukraine on Tuesday accused Russia of committing a war crime after a video was released showing a drone chasing down and wounding a vegetable seller in the southern Ukrainian city of Kherson.

Footage released by Ukrainian police ‌shows the drone pursuing a man around a van being used as a street stand before exploding as he dives for ‌cover behind the vehicle. Police said the man in his 50s survived but suffered shock and shrapnel injuries.

Ukrainian officials later identified him only as a 52-year-old called Yurii and released ​a video interview with him from a hospital ward.

"Today, many were shocked by yet another video of the drone 'safari' Russians are carrying out against civilians in Kherson," President Volodymyr Zelenskiy wrote on X, saying that "Russia has gone mad" and calling for more pressure on Moscow and strong security guarantees for Ukraine.

"We must act and support life in ways that force Russia to think seriously about peace rather than expanding the range of its drones."

Russia's Defence Ministry did not immediately respond to Reuters request for comment ⁠on the incident.

The vegetable seller went to Kherson in the morning to sell produce, said Oleksandr Prokudin, head of the Kherson regional military administration. Prokudin released the video interview with the man on the Telegram app.

"I only just put up the umbrella and started unloading the boxes. My wife was there, ​too. ​Then we heard it buzzing but could not even see it. It came ​from somewhere behind the market, from those bushes over there, ‌and flew in very low," said Yurii, sitting in a hospital ward.

"It is open steppe. There is nowhere to go. It is terrifying, of course. Really terrifying."

On the video, Yurii showed his wounds on both legs and also on his back. His wife ran off and was not injured, he said.

Sybiha said the attack formed part of a deliberate Russian campaign to intimidate civilians. "This barbaric Russian war crime in Kherson demands international condemnation and justice, but thousands of similar crimes never come to the public eye," he wrote on Telegram.

In July, the U.N. Human Rights Monitoring Mission ‌in Ukraine said it had documented 1,396 civilian deaths and 7,978 injuries in ​the first six months of 2026, marking a 37% increase from 2025 and more than ​double the figures from 2024.

It said that the surge in ​civilian casualties was primarily driven by intensifying Russian long-range missile and drone strikes targeting cities far from the front ‌lines.

Ukraine is also attacking Russia with drones and long-range missiles, ​many of which have caused civilian ​casualties, Russian authorities say.

Russia on Monday accused Ukraine of terrorism after seven people, including three children, were killed at its Black Sea holiday resort of Gelendzhik in what it said was a deliberate Ukrainian drone attack on civilians.

A Ukrainian official said that the drone ​only fell on the beach in Gelendzhik because ‌it was shot down by Russian air defences, adding that "Ukraine uses its weapons exclusively against the Russian military-industrial complex and economic ​infrastructure facilities".

Both Russia and Ukraine deny targeting civilians in the war triggered by Russia's invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

(Reporting ​by Aleksandar Vasovic, Olena Harmash; Editing by Ros Russell and Hugh Lawson)

title: Ukraine says missile interceptor deliveries have fallen to third of 2025 level
description: Allies have supplied just a third of the air defence missiles to Ukraine in 2026 compared with 2025, President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said on Wednesday, as Russia escalates
fullText:
KYIV, Aug 5 (Reuters) - Allies have supplied just a third of the air defence missiles to Ukraine in 2026 compared with 2025, President ‌Volodymyr Zelenskiy said on Wednesday, as Russia escalates strikes on the capital ‌of Kyiv and its southern port hub.

Ukraine has been short on U.S.-made Patriot interceptors capable of ​downing Russian ballistic missiles since the start of the war. But in recent weeks, the acute shortage came into focus, with Moscow pummelling Kyiv, on average, every three days in July alone.

"And this is not just a summer phenomenon - it applies to ‌every period of the first ⁠half of 2026," Zelenskiy added on the Telegram app.

In what has become a pattern in recent weeks, Ukrainian air defences failed ⁠to intercept a single one of the 24 ballistic missiles and four Zircon cruise missiles during Wednesday's attack, the air force said.

Serhii Beskrestnov, an adviser to Ukraine's president ​on the ​development of defence technology, estimates that Russia ​is capable of launching 100 ‌ballistic missiles every month to attack logistic hubs, industrial facilities, food and building warehouses.

"The war of attrition has entered its next phase," he said on the Telegram app.

In addition to its own capabilities, Russia again turned to the deployment of North Korean missiles. Last week, Moscow's troops fired the first two North Korean missiles ‌since last August, Ukraine said.

A North Korean missile ​unit has begun deploying to western Russia and ​could be equipped with 120 ​ballistic missiles and six launchers, according to Ukraine's military intelligence.

With ‌interceptor stocks limited across the globe and ​political volatility affecting ​supplies, one possible way for Ukraine to counteract is to target Russian missile launchers, some military analysts say.

Ukraine's current capabilities do not permit such strikes. ​Kyiv is also pressing ‌allies to develop a pan-European anti-ballistic system and has sought a licence ​from the U.S. to produce Patriot missiles itself.

title: Why Trump is downplaying reports Russia and China are helping Iran
description: Trump says he'll ask Putin directly about satellite imagery allegations as experts warn Russia and China are quietly aiding Iran against U.S. forces.
fullText:
President Donald Trump cast doubt in recent days on allegations that Russia is helping Iran target U.S. forces, even as members of his own administration acknowledge Moscow and Beijing are supporting Tehran in other ways.

Trump dismissed Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's claim that Russia supplied Iran with satellite imagery of U.S. military installations in the Gulf, saying any assistance would have been "very unimpactful" given the damage inflicted on Iran's military.

"We'll find out if that's true. I'll ask Putin. We'll find out," Trump told reporters at the end of July.

Waltz Warns Of Chinese, Russian-fueled 'National Security Threat' Looming Close To Us Shores

"I don't think they've been doing it, certainly not at a high level," Trump added. "And if they have, it has been very unimpactful."

Trump pointed to the damage Iran's military has suffered during the war. Russian help, he argued, has failed to stop the United States from destroying much of Tehran's conventional forces.

Trump's comments came as his administration confronted separate reports that Russia and China are helping Iran in different ways — allegations that, if borne out, would suggest America's two chief geopolitical rivals are quietly supporting a nation at war with the U.S. Members of his own administration have acknowledged broader help from Moscow and Beijing.

China's Iran Ties Complicate Trump-xi Summit As Tensions Test Us Leverage

War Secretary Pete Hegseth has said Russia and China are "enabling some of the things Iran is doing," but a White House official told Fox News Digital that any foreign assistance has failed to improve Tehran's ability to attack Americans.

Trump's comments came in response to two recent reports: Zelenskyy's allegation that Russia provided satellite intelligence to Iran and a Reuters report that China could send hundreds of shoulder-fired air-defense missiles to Tehran through Pakistan, which China has denied.

Fresh satellite imagery could help Iran locate high-value assets and refine strike coordinates, then show whether an attack hit its intended target.

"As the President stated, nothing that any outside actor is doing to help Iran is in any way increasing their ability to target Americans," the official told Fox News Digital, responding to questions about Zelenskyy's claim that Russia gave Iran satellite imagery of U.S. military installations in the Gulf.

Zelenskyy laid out Ukraine's evidence Saturday, saying Russian satellites had surveyed Gulf countries and U.S. military installations beginning in early July before the imagery later appeared in Iran.

"These images subsequently appear in Iran," Zelenskyy wrote on X.

Ukraine found what Zelenskyy described as a "clear correlation" between the Russian observations and subsequent Iranian attacks. According to Zelenskyy, Moscow collected imagery before strikes to aid targeting and returned afterward to assess the damage.

Zelenskyy said Russian satellites focused on four air bases over two days — two in Bahrain and one each in Jordan and Kuwait — and said Ukrainian intelligence had shared the information with foreign partners.

Ukrainian Ambassador to the U.S. Olga Stefanishyna said at a July 30 reporter roundtable that the allegation did not arise during Zelenskyy's White House meeting with Trump because the agenda was crowded. She said Ukraine had provided the information "through other channels."

A Ukrainian official told Fox News Digital that Kyiv wants to avoid "opening a second front" with Iran.

Hegseth acknowledged Russian and Chinese support for Iran during a Senate hearing in July.

There was "definitely adversary alignment," Hegseth said. Russia and China were "at different levels, enabling some of the things Iran is doing."

The U.S. has ways to deter that support, he added, though some of those measures should remain classified. Hegseth said earlier in the war that the administration knew "exactly" what Moscow and Beijing were doing and was addressing their actions where needed.

Russia has denied supplying Iran with intelligence on American military targets. Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said the locations of U.S. bases were publicly available. The Kremlin also dismissed earlier reporting about Russian intelligence support for Iran as false.

Trump also questioned reports that Iran could soon receive hundreds of Chinese-made shoulder-fired air-defense systems through Pakistan, saying Chinese President Xi Jinping had assured him Beijing would stay out of the conflict.

"That was surprising. I mean, things like that happen, but that would be surprising. He told me very strongly he wouldn't partake, but he knows I'd be quite disappointed. He's coming here, I think, on September 24," the president told reporters Wednesday.

Matthew Kroenig, a former Pentagon and intelligence official, called the reports "highly plausible," pointing to growing cooperation among Russia, China and Iran.

"From Russia and China's point of view, if they can complicate the U.S. war in the Middle East and raise the cost to Washington, that's a good thing for them," Kroenig told Fox News Digital.

Kroenig said Trump may be warning Moscow and Beijing privately instead of confronting them before television cameras.

"That might be the most generous interpretation, that it's his way of warning China and Russia to knock it off," he said.

Trump's comments would carry more risk if the president were relying on assurances from Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping, Kroenig said. He urged the administration to make clear that either country would face a cost for helping Tehran.

"I think there would be a risk to just discounting this altogether," Kroenig said.

Anna Borshchevskaya, a senior fellow at the Washington Institute for Near East Policy, said Moscow has spent years building closer military ties with Tehran.

"If this proves accurate, Russia has found a way to help Iran without direct military engagement, and that's why this is significant," Borshchevskaya told Fox News Digital.

Iran began supplying Russia with Shahed attack drones in 2022, giving Moscow a cheap weapon it could launch in waves against Ukrainian cities and power infrastructure.

Russia later began producing its own versions with Iranian support and improved the design, making the drones a mainstay of its attacks. Tehran's earlier support now hangs over Zelenskyy's claim that Moscow is helping Iran target American forces.

Satellite imagery would give Moscow another way to aid Tehran while avoiding a direct clash with American forces.

"It's hard to think how the provision of intelligence is insignificant," Borshchevskaya said.

She said Trump may be trying to keep his public exchanges with Moscow calm as U.S. officials send firmer messages in private.

Russia views the wars in Ukraine and Iran as connected parts of its campaign against American influence, Borshchevskaya said. U.S. officials tend to handle each conflict through a separate policy process.

"The challenge for us is that we often separate theaters, but Russia does not," she said. "Russia looks at all of these conflicts in a much more interconnected way."

Borshchevskaya said Russia has chosen forms of aid that can strengthen Iran without committing Russian troops or entering a direct fight with Washington.

"Russia is being restrained here," she said. "They're playing a much more nuanced game."

Trump also voiced surprise Wednesday at a report that Iran could soon receive hundreds of Chinese-made, shoulder-fired air-defense systems through Pakistan.

Xi had given Trump a firm assurance that China would stay out of the war, according to the president.

"He told me very strongly he wouldn't partake, but he knows I'd be quite disappointed," Trump said.

China called the report "groundless." Pakistan rejected the claim that it would help route the weapons to Iran, calling the allegation "baseless and devoid of truth."

Kroenig said Beijing has supplied Russia with economic and industrial support during the war in Ukraine. China has stopped short of openly sending lethal weapons, a limit he had expected Beijing to observe in the Iran war.

Advanced air defenses would require approval from the Chinese government, he said. Russian satellite intelligence would also come from state-controlled capabilities.

"There are no mom-and-pop shops in St. Petersburg selling this data," Kroenig said.

MOSCOW, Aug 4 (Reuters) - Ukrainian drones hit three warehouses in Russia in overnight attacks that killed five people, local officials said on Tuesday, as the strikes intensify pressure ‌on the operations of online retailer Wildberries.

Often described as Russia's answer to Amazon, Wildberries has ‌become a frequent target of Ukrainian attacks in recent weeks, part of what Kyiv says is a campaign to bring ​the war home to ordinary Russians.

The company said fire crews were containing a blaze after the latest attack struck one of its warehouses near St Petersburg. In the Tver region, northwest of Moscow, drones damaged another Wildberries facility, local authorities said. Local authorities reported no casualties in either of the strikes.

But in the ‌Moscow region, a drone attack on ⁠the city of Chekhov set another warehouse alight and damaged an electrical substation and another building, killing five people and injuring 10, the governor, Andrei Vorobyov, ⁠said. He did not say which company the site belonged to or specify exactly where the deaths had occurred.

Since launching its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Russia has repeatedly struck Ukrainian logistics hubs as well ​as ​other infrastructure.

Ukraine has expanded its own long-range drone strategy, ​targeting close to 20 Wildberries sites since ‌July 18. The strikes have inflicted significant damage on a company that has become a driving force in Russia's retail sector, processing millions of orders a day through vast warehouses spread across the country.

All stock at a large Wildberries warehouse in the Samara region was destroyed after a strike on Sunday sparked a fire that gutted the facility, state news agency TASS quoted regional official Denis Gurkov ‌as saying on Tuesday.

"Of its 180,000 square metres, 160,000 ​burned down," he said. That is roughly equivalent to 22 ​soccer pitches.

On Monday, hundreds of firefighters worked ​to put out a 100,000-square-metre fire at a Wildberries warehouse in the Vladimir ‌region. Only part of its stock was saved, ​the company said, without ​giving further details.

Wildberries has not given an estimate of the financial losses resulting so far from the attacks, which founder and CEO Tatyana Kim has described as "acts of terrorism."

The company, which ​also operates in Central Asia ‌and the Caucasus, is building 260,000 square metres of warehouse capacity in neighbouring Kazakhstan, the ​Kazakh trade minister said on Tuesday.

title: Ukraine has drones that can lock onto targets when Russia severs the connection to their operators, letting them complete their attacks
description: Russian jamming can sever Ukrainian pilots' drone links, but target-lock technology can still guide the drones to their targets.
fullText:
Many of Ukraine's drones can lock onto targets and strike even after operator control is lost.

That kind of autonomy helps Ukraine fight through Russian jamming and make better use of limited manpower.

Most drones use only limited automation, but Ukraine is investing heavily in greater autonomy.

Ukraine is fighting with drones that lock onto their targets when they lose connection with their human operators.

Dmytro "Liber" Zhluktenko, a former drone operator who is now a lessons-learned analyst with Ukraine's 413th Unmanned Systems Regiment "RAID," told Business Insider that many of the country's drones use what he called "target lock," which allows drones to continue on to find and hit their targets even when their operators lose control.

It's "quite useful," he said, especially considering that Ukrainian operators frequently experience signal loss before they hit their targets due to Russian electronic warfare and also because of the ways many drones are designed.

The "target lock" capability is used on systems such as Perennial Autonomy's Hornet mid-range strike drone. The drone communicates with its operator through a SpaceX-made Starlink terminal mounted onboard, Zhluktenko said. However, deep dives and aggressive maneuvers sometimes interrupt the Starlink connection, causing the antenna to lose the satellite lock, he said.

Giving drones that kind of target lock, allowing operators to "have the autonomy to do the rest of the work, is just great," Zhluktenko said.

Ukraine isn't fighting with fully automated weaponry. Humans remain largely in control and responsible for selecting targets. That creates challenges as Russia's electronic warfare affects operations by disrupting GPS and cutting the command and video links connecting drones to their operators. That's where the limited but useful autonomy comes into play.

Ukraine also sees autonomy as a way for its smaller military to take on Russia, reducing the number of decisions each operator must make and potentially allowing one person to manage more systems simultaneously.

A growing number of drones in Ukraine operate with a human identifying and selecting a target, then designating it for the drone's camera and guidance software. The drone's technology can then adjust its course to continue tracking the target. If jamming or other interference cuts the video feed or command link, the drone can still continue toward the target the operator selected.

The sophistication of that terminal guidance varies. It may involve a pre-programmed process or a more advanced system that uses artificial intelligence. But the ability to continue operating without constant human input is increasingly important.

Zhluktenko said that some systems are "able to navigate themselves and fly by the route without human input" by matching imagery from their cameras with stored satellite maps.

But all of the currently deployed systems on the battlefield "have a human in the loop to a very significant extent," he added.

Early forms of this kind of targeting technology aboard attack drones were observed in June 2025, when Ukrainian forces executed Operation Spiderweb. Ukraine reported that the attack, which involved sneaking drones close to the target positions in trucks, hit 41 Russian aircraft stationed at bases. Ukraine said that when some of the drones lost signal, they used AI to continue along their pre-planned route and have their warheads automatically activate upon finding their targets.

Ukraine is promoting this technology. Its defense ministry, for example, has highlighted the work of Ukrainian company F-Drones, which makes the LITAVR drone. The ministry says that the drone has an automatic terminal-guidance system that "identifies the target and autonomously guides the drone to impact."

"During the terminal phase of flight," the ministry said, the operator "controls only the speed, while all other functions are performed automatically."

Ukrainian companies are also making equipment that can attach to multiple types of drones and provide similar capabilities. The company The Fourth Law makes its TFL-1 terminal-guidance module, which allows a human operator to select the drone's target before machine vision locks onto and tracks it. That allows the drone to complete its final attack even if the operator's connection is lost.

Mykyta Rozhkov, the chief business development officer of Ukrainian drone and weapons maker Frontline Robotics, told Business Insider that many drones in Ukraine can navigate autonomously toward targets operators have identified.

That is helpful when the signal drops, but autonomy could also help Ukraine manage a rapidly growing fleet of drones and robots. "You need some level of autonomy in order to achieve it," he said.

Many companies see autonomy as a way for smaller militaries to field more systems without requiring an equivalent increase in personnel. Latvian drone maker Origin Robotics, which supplies Ukraine, makes the Blaze interceptor drone. The company says it uses radar-based detection and AI-powered computer vision for autonomous target acquisition and interception, while humans still confirm whether to engage.

In this case, the autonomy is not intended to let the drone strike after communication is lost. The drone self-destructs if its connection is severed. CEO Agris Kipurs told Business Insider that autonomy is important for smaller militaries like Latvia's or Ukraine's because it allows them to effectively scale. "We don't have the numbers in terms of infantry," he said.

Ukraine is supporting the development of more autonomous weapons. Brave1, a Ukrainian government-backed defense technology platform and accelerator, said last year that autonomous detection and destruction of targets "is critical to preserving resources and increasing combat effectiveness."

"The key role is played by the time between target detection and destruction," the operation said.

The amount of autonomy in weaponry varies widely. Bohdan Sas, the president and cofounder of Ukrainian defense company Buntar Aerospace, told Business Insider that some companies have been "able to automate some simple tasks. For example, final target acquisition and final targeting is relatively easy."

Buntar makes drones and software that use optical navigation and other tools to operate in areas affected by electronic warfare.

Sas said developers can use software such as OpenCV, a widely used open-source computer-vision library, alongside a machine-learning algorithm to "automate a small step," allowing the drone to recognize and track a target with its camera and steer toward it.

Ukraine is pledging to further strengthen the autonomy of its weapons. Ukraine's defense ministry said in June that a company had developed technology that automated 95% of an interceptor drone's engagement cycle: A human operator selects a target and tells the drone to engage, while the system autonomously identifies the enemy drone, tracks it, and conducts the intercept.

Ukraine's then-defense minister, Mykhailo Fedorov, said in March that "in modern warfare, we must defeat Russia in every technological cycle. Artificial intelligence is one of the key areas of this competition."

"The future of warfare belongs to autonomous systems. Our task is to enhance the autonomy of drones and other combat systems so that they can detect targets more quickly, analyze the situation, and help inform decisions on the battlefield."

For now, most Ukrainian systems appear to use narrower forms of automation, with human operators selecting targets and onboard software handling tasks such as recognition, tracking, navigation, or terminal guidance. But many in the industry predict rapid progress.

Rozhkov said Frontline expects "not fully autonomous, but pretty much autonomous operations done by robots in real battlefield conditions in 12 months."

If you enjoyed this story, be sure to follow Business Insider on Yahoo.

title: Ukraine accuses Russia of war crime after video shows drone attacking market vendor
description: Ukraine on Tuesday accused Russia of committing a war crime after a video was released showing a drone chasing down and wounding a street vendor in the southern Ukrainian city
fullText:
KYIV, Aug 4 (Reuters) - Ukraine on Tuesday accused Russia of committing a war crime after a video was released showing a drone chasing down and wounding a street vendor in the southern Ukrainian ‌city of Kherson.

Footage released by Ukrainian police shows the drone pursuing an unidentified man around a van ‌being used as a street stand before exploding after he dives for cover behind the vehicle. Police said the vendor, a man in his ​50s, survived but suffered shock and shrapnel injuries.

"Today, many were shocked by yet another video of the drone 'safari' Russians are carrying out against civilians in Kherson," President Volodymyr Zelenskiy wrote on X, issuing a fresh call for more pressure on Russia and strong security guarantees for Ukraine.

"We must act and support life in ways that force Russia to think seriously about ‌peace rather than expanding the range of ⁠its drones."

Sybiha said the attack formed part of a deliberate Russian campaign to intimidate civilians. "This barbaric Russian war crime in Kherson demands international condemnation and justice, but thousands of similar crimes never come to the public ​eye," ​he wrote on Telegram.

The minister said the pilot of the Russian ​drone would have been aware they were targeting ‌a civilian, branding them a "sadist".

Two children and an elderly woman were also killed in overnight Russian guided bomb strikes on Ukraine's northern city of Sumy, regional governor Oleh Hryhorov said on Telegram.

In July, the U.N. Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine said it had documented 1,396 civilian deaths and 7,978 injuries in the first six months of 2026, marking a 37% increase from 2025 and more than double the figures from 2024.

It said that the surge in civilian ‌casualties was primarily driven by intensifying Russian long-range missile and drone ​strikes targeting urban centres far beyond the front lines.

Ukraine is also attacking ​Russia with drones and long-range missiles, many of ​which have also caused civilian casualties, Russian authorities say.

Russia on Monday accused Ukraine of terrorism ‌after seven people, including three children, were killed and ​60 injured at its Black ​Sea holiday resort of Gelendzhik in what it said was a deliberate Ukrainian drone attack on civilians.

A Ukrainian official said that the drone only fell on the beach in Gelendzhik because it was shot down by ​Russian air defences, adding that "Ukraine uses ‌its weapons exclusively against the Russian military-industrial complex and economic infrastructure facilities".

Both Russia and Ukraine deny targeting ​civilians in the war triggered by Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

title: A Putin critic leaves Russia after he is barred him from running for parliament
description: Opposition politician Boris Nadezhdin, who criticized Russia's war in Ukraine and tried to challenge President Vladimir Putin in the 2024 election, said Monday he has left Russia, a move that follows ...
fullText:
Opposition politician Boris Nadezhdin, who criticized Russia's war in Ukraine and tried to challenge President Vladimir Putin in the 2024 election, said Monday he has left Russia, a move that follows a crackdown that barred him from a race for parliament this year.

Nadezhdin, 63, shared a video on Telegram, showing him standing in front of the Eiffel Tower in Paris.

"Good news: I'm alive and free. Unfortunately, not in Russia for the time being," he said, adding that he needs "to look around and figure out life going forward."

In July, a Russian court fined Nadezhdin about $13 for displaying "extremist symbols," charges that he rejected as absurd. The accusations stemmed from a 2023 online video that briefly showed a picture of the late opposition leader Alexei Navalny, convicted of extremism in a case widely seen as politically motivated.

Earlier that month, Nadezhdin also was designated a "foreign agent" — a label that brings additional government scrutiny as well as stigmatizing connotations in Russia.

That and a fine on an extremism-related charge barred him from running in September's parliamentary vote, which is expected to be tightly controlled by the Kremlin.

The ruling United Russia party is seeking to preserve its dominance in the lower house of parliament in a race against the Communist Party and a couple of other parties that vote in sync with the Kremlin on key issues. The campaign comes amid signs of growing public fatigue with the war in Ukraine as fuel shortages and economic pain increase, an environment that reduces the authorities' tolerance for even token opposition.

In January 2024, Nadezhdin collected thousands of signatures in his run for president as he openly called for an end to the war in Ukraine. But he was kept off the March 2024 ballot after Russia's Supreme Court ruled that more than 9,000 signatures submitted by his campaign were invalid — enough to disqualify him. Putin faced only token opposition in the election and easily gained a fifth term.

A veteran politician, Nadezhdin worked in the government in the 1990s when he was an adviser to Sergei Kiriyenko, now a top Putin aide. He also served as a lawmaker and more recently became a member of a municipal council. He was one of the few high-profile Putin critics still living in Russia.

Earlier this year, Nadezhdin declared his bid to run for the lower house of parliament, the State Duma, and vowed to continue his symbolic campaign even after the Justice Ministry branded him with the "foreign agent" designation.

Another blow came when police briefly detained Nadezhdin and charged him with displaying "extremist symbols." The politician said he was considering a move abroad but was barred from leaving Russia. It wasn't clear from his Monday video statement whether the ban has since been lifted, or if he left the country despite it.

After the Kremlin's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, authorities ramped up their crackdown on dissent and free speech, relentlessly targeting rights organizations, independent media, members of civil society organizations and Kremlin critics. Hundreds of people have been jailed and thousands of others fled the country.

title: 'The damage is enormous': Ukraine grapples with record-breaking Russian strikes
description: Russia launched 381 missiles into Ukraine in July, Kyiv said.
fullText:
Russia set new wartime records for the rate and scale of its missile strikes on Ukrainian cities in July, according to data published by the Ukrainian air force and analyzed by ABC News, as the Ukrainian government accelerated its efforts to patch well-publicized gaps in its aerial defensive umbrella.

Across July, Russia launched a total of 381 missiles of all types into Ukraine, the air force in Kyiv said, at a rate of just over 12 per day -- setting new wartime records for the overall number and rate of missiles launched into the country.

The data also indicated that missiles have become a more prominent element of Russia's nightly -- and sometimes also daytime -- combined strikes, which are largely comprised of drones. In July, though, the proportion of Russian missiles in the overall munition count increased to a record high of just over 7%, according to Ukrainian air force data analyzed by ABC News.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, his top officials and military commanders have been clear on Kyiv's struggle to intercept Russian missiles, particularly of the ballistic variety, which fly at speeds and attack at angles that make it more difficult to shoot them down.

Ukraine's deep strikes mean 'significant change' for war, former Russian PM says

In July, the Ukrainian air force reported a Russian missile failure rate -- including munitions that were intercepted, suppressed or failed to reach their targets -- of around 58%. For ballistic missiles -- including Iskander-M and S-400 missiles, which the air force often groups together in its after action reports -- the failure rate was around 28%.

Ukraine's air force publishes daily tallies of Russian drone and missile strikes, including information as to how many munitions were intercepted and how many penetrated air defenses. The air force includes a wide range of missile types in its count, sometimes including the "Banderol" low-cost cruise missile.

Moscow publishes only the number of Ukrainian drones and other projectiles it claims to have intercepted.

ABC News cannot independently verify the data released by either Ukraine or Russia. It is possible that both Kyiv and Moscow may seek to exaggerate the effectiveness of their air defenses, or to amplify the attacks against them.

Neither side provides detailed data on the number of munitions used in their own attacks. Both Kyiv and Moscow routinely describe their targets as military, energy or industrial sites and both accuse the other of intentionally attacking civilian targets.

'Trump does like a winner': Ukraine victories could mean more US backing, Zelenskyy adviser says

The U.S.-made Patriot surface-to-air missile system has become Ukraine's prime defense against such munitions, but a global shortage of interceptor missiles -- exacerbated by the ongoing U.S.-Israeli war with Iran -- and President Donald Trump's decision to wind down U.S. aid to Kyiv has put severe strain on Ukrainian defenses, officials said.

Kyiv is also working to produce its own homegrown interceptor missile -- the Freyja -- and collaborating with European partners to use it in a shared anti-ballistic missile shield. Kyiv is targeting early 2027 for a Freyja prototype, officials have said.

Two sit-downs with Trump this month initially produced good news for Kyiv. During warm bilateral meetings with Zelenskyy at the NATO summit in Ankara, Turkey, and later at the White House, Trump said he would give Ukraine permission to produce Patriot interceptors on Ukrainian soil.

Ukraine scales up drone attacks in Moscow, across Russia to record highs, data shows

Zelenskyy described the decision as a "historic political agreement," but warned later that there could be no immediate fix.

After visiting the White House for talks in late July, Zelenskyy said Ukraine was seeking the delivery of another 300 Patriot interceptor missiles to bolster its defenses before next winter.

Trump declined to provide any new missiles and even walked back his commitment to providing Ukraine a Patriot production license. "We have not agreed to that. We're talking about it, but it's a hard thing to give away that kind of technology," the president said during a Cabinet meeting at Camp David last week.

The Patriot is Ukraine's most potent weapon in its ongoing cat-and-mouse game with Russia, analysts say, in which both sides are constantly adapting to gain an edge over the other.

Russian missiles have been seen employing defensive measures, like deploying flares just before impact to misdirect interceptor missiles, and Moscow routinely changes its directions and timings of attack, Olha Polishchuk of the ACLED conflict monitoring organization told ABC News.

NATO ally Romania reports increased rate of Russian drone incursions, fighter alerts

But Moscow is facing its own logistical pressures as it expands its long-range attacks, according to Ukrainian Air Force spokesperson Yuriy Ihnat. He said last month that some of Russia's ballistic missiles were launched into Ukraine just weeks after coming off the factory production line, perhaps indicating that Russia's stockpiles are dwindling.

In June, Ukraine's military intelligence said that Russian forces could launch up to 100 ballistic missiles each month without exhausting its stockpiles. In July, Ukraine's air force said Russia launched at least 126 such missiles, which may represent an unsustainable tempo if Kyiv's estimates prove correct.

Russia's use of a North Korean ballistic missile in strikes in late July might also indicate its production pressures, Ukrainian officials said.

"Now, Russia sees that it's effective, it exploits it as much as possible," Polishchuk said of Moscow's ballistic strikes. "But it will have to stop at some point to again accumulate those missiles, to then again launch similar attacks. Until Ukraine becomes effective in intercepting them, which will likely take a while."

Through Ukraine's hot summer, the human toll of Russia's long-range attacks is mounting.

Through July, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said the Ukrainian capital was hit by 11 combined missile and drone attacks, killing at least 56 people and wounding another 220 people.

Russian missile violated NATO airspace in Poland, Kyiv says, amid deadly strikes

The last week of July saw Ukrainian cities suffer two major missile attacks, in which at least 17 people were killed. After a deadly attack on July 31, Zelenskyy wrote on X, "Only one ballistic missile was intercepted, simply because there are no interceptors for the Patriot systems."

When the missiles do come, Polishchuk said, air raid sirens and SMS alerts give residents only two to four minutes of warning, "Not enough time to get to a shelter," she said. Civilians have no indication of where the missile may land, she added, given that Russian missiles regularly strike residential buildings as well as infrastructure and military targets.

"There is very little incoming noise, and then 'boom,'" Ivan Stupak, a military analyst and a former officer in the Security Service of Ukraine, told ABC News from Kyiv. The short warning time causes "enormous stress," he added, recalling that the last missile attack on the capital came at 1:30 a.m. local time and "caught me off guard."

"Then you are trying to find your clothes and jump in the shelter," Stupak said.

In reversal, Trump says he hasn't 'agreed to' grant Ukraine licenses to produce Patriot missiles

Serhiy Kiral, the deputy mayor of Lviv,  told ABC News that the damage wrought by a ballistic missile strike is "enormous." Last week's impact caused tens of millions of Ukrainian hryvnias in damages, Kiral said, saw dozens of people placed in temporary housing and prompted some 500 people to request aid from government support centers.

Even for those who escape death or injury, Kiral said, homes and businesses can be "erased" in seconds and the subsequent psychological trauma can prove a years-long challenge.

The United Nations' monitoring mission in Ukraine said last month that it was seeing a "disturbing escalation" in the nature of Russian attacks. June, it said, was the deadliest month for civilians in the country since the opening months of the war in early 2022, with at least 293 civilians killed and 1,990 others injured.

Russia sets new record for drone, missile attacks on Ukraine in April

The mission said that the increase was largely driven by long-range Russian attacks.

Residents of Kherson -- a southern Ukrainian city which sits along the Dnipro River, which since late 2022 has served as the front line in the southern theater -- are under constant fire, one humanitarian volunteer there told ABC News.

The city "is truly in hell," Natalia Sergienko, director of the Kherson Power of the South public organization, said, "The city is almost daily subjected to artillery shelling, guided bomb strikes and drone attacks." Drones pose a particular threat, Sergienko said, routinely attacking civilians, cars and humanitarian transport vehicles.

"Every day people die from enemy shells. It is impossible to live for years under constant shelling, hearing explosions, losing acquaintances, seeing human pain and remaining the same as before," she said.

Aug 2 (Reuters) - Ukrainian drone strikes killed at least eight people in Russian regions overnight and on Sunday, hitting targets including a warehouse belonging to Wildberries, Russia's largest online retailer, ‌regional officials said.

Russia's Defence Ministry said it had downed 635 Ukrainian drones during the night.

Kyiv's ‌drones attacked a Wildberries warehouse in the Samara region, around 800 km (500 miles) from Ukraine's most advanced military positions, Samara Governor ​Vyacheslav Fedorishchev said. He said there were no casualties and that a fire that had broken out as a result of the attack was being put out.

Ukrainian forces have been hitting deeper inside Russia as they expand strikes on economic and energy targets, aiming to undermine Moscow's ability to wage its more than four-year-old war in ‌Ukraine.

They have attacked about a dozen ⁠Wildberries sites since July 18 in an attempt to disrupt the operations of the company, a linchpin of the consumer economy often described as Russia's version of ⁠Amazon.

A strike on a residential building in the neighbouring Saratov region killed two people in the city of Engels, Governor Roman Busargin said. Civil infrastructure was damaged both in Engels and in the city of Saratov, he said.

Both ​Saratov city, ​which hosts a major oil refinery, and Engels, home ​of a military airbase, have come under ‌repeated Ukrainian attack in recent years.

Kyiv's military said on Sunday that Ukrainian forces had attacked the Saratov refinery and the Engels airbase, sparking fires at both facilities. It said its forces had also struck an oil depot in the western Kaluga region.

Three people were killed and two injured in a drone attack on the Udmurtia region of Russia, acting governor Olga Abramova said. In the border region of Belgorod, three people ‌were killed and five injured in Ukrainian strikes, the local ​task force reported.

The governor of Russia's Bashkortostan region, Radiy Khabirov, ​said air defence units had repelled a ​massive drone attack on industrial facilities. One of the drones was shot down over ‌the industrial area of the regional capital of ​Ufa and a fire ​was being put out, he said.

Russia's Defence Ministry said its forces had struck infrastructure and two vessels with military cargo in the Ukrainian port of Mykolaiv, as well as a vessel carrying ​military supplies in the Black Sea.

In ‌the southeastern Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia, regional governor Ivan Fedorov said Russian-launched glide bombs killed ​one person and injured 21.
